title: Free BrowserStack Alternatives: What You Can Test Without Paying
metaTitle: Free BrowserStack Alternatives: 8 Options That Work
description: Free BrowserStack alternatives for developers and testers: browser tools, simulators, Playwright and free cloud tiers, and what each one misses.

image.alt: Free BrowserStack alternatives. Card reading: free tools cover most of it, real devices cover the rest

blocks.v: The best free BrowserStack alternatives depend on what you need to test. For layout at phone sizes, your browser's own tools are enough. For Safari on an iPhone, a Mac with Xcode gets you close. For automated tests across browsers, Playwright is free and open source. For real devices, free options exist, but they are limited.
This guide covers free options only. If you are choosing between two paid platforms, see [[BrowserStack vs LambdaTest|/browserstack-vs-lambdatest]] instead.
What can free BrowserStack alternatives replace?

BrowserStack's value comes from two things: real devices and browsers you do not own, and a grid for running automated tests in parallel. Free tools can replace much of the second and some of the first. What they cannot easily replace is a real iPhone or Android phone with its real hardware.

blocks.v: 1. Browser device modes in Chrome, Firefox and Safari

Every major desktop browser has a mode that resizes the page to phone and tablet sizes. Chrome calls it device mode, and Firefox and Safari call it Responsive Design Mode. You can pick common devices, rotate them and slow the network down.

The limit is the engine. Chrome's device mode still renders with Chrome on your computer, and Google's own documentation describes it as a first-order approximation of a mobile device. Safari's Responsive Design Mode on a Mac is closer for iPhone checks, because it uses WebKit, the engine every iPhone browser uses outside the EU.
2. Xcode's iOS Simulator

Apple's Xcode, free from the Mac App Store, includes a Simulator that runs simulated iPhones and iPads with Safari. It is the closest free way to see a site as an iPhone user does, and you can inspect pages in it with Safari's Web Inspector on the Mac.
There are catches. It needs a Mac, it is a large download, and it simulates rather than reproduces the hardware, so performance and some device behaviour will not match a real phone.
3. Android Studio's emulator

Android Studio is free and includes an emulator that runs Android system images. You can create virtual devices at different screen sizes and Android versions, then open your site in Chrome. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

It is very good for checking older Android versions, which many visitors still use. It does not reproduce every manufacturer's changes to Android, so a Samsung or Xiaomi phone may still behave differently.
4. Playwright for automated cross-browser testing

Playwright is an open source testing framework from Microsoft. One set of tests can run on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and it can emulate mobile screen sizes, touch and device settings. It is free, and it runs on your own machine or in a CI pipeline such as GitHub Actions.

Its documentation is clear that its WebKit build is not the same as branded Safari, and it recommends running WebKit on a Mac for the closest results to Safari. Even so, it catches many Safari-specific problems before they reach a real device. For many small teams, Playwright in CI replaces most of what they would otherwise pay a cloud grid for.
5. Selenium Grid on your own machines

Selenium is the long-standing open source browser automation project, and Selenium Grid lets you run tests across several machines and browsers at once. It is free, but the servers, the browsers and the maintenance are yours. It is the do-it-yourself version of a testing cloud, and it makes sense mainly for teams with someone to look after it.
6. The TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) free plan
LambdaTest renamed itself TestMu AI in January 2026. As of November 2026, its pricing page lists free-forever tiers that need no credit card:

v: Live: a few short live testing sessions of about two minutes each, renewed monthly, including a small number of real device sessions.
Automation: 100 minutes of web and mobile automation with 2 parallel sessions, a one-time allowance that does not renew.
SmartUI visual testing: 2,000 screenshots, also a one-time allowance.

blocks.v: Two-minute sessions are enough to confirm a bug, not to test a whole site, so think of it as a permanent trial. The pricing page describes the Live limits slightly differently in different places, so check them yourself.
TestMu AI pricing (official page)
The free tiers sit alongside the paid plans on the same page, grouped by live testing, automation, HyperExecute, visual testing and accessibility.
7. BrowserStack's own free options
BrowserStack itself has three free routes, each narrow:

v: A free trial, which its support pages put at 30 minutes of Live, 60 minutes of Automate and 30 minutes of App Live.
Percy's free plan, with 5,000 visual testing screenshots a month as of November 2026.
A free programme for open source projects, covering Live, Automate and Percy with 5 users and 5 parallel sessions.

blocks.v: If you maintain an open source project, apply for that programme before looking anywhere else.
BrowserStack pricing (official page)

Sauce Labs, another paid testing cloud, offers a 28-day free trial at the time of writing and may ask for payment details at sign-up. Like any trial, it is a way to evaluate a product, not a free alternative.
8. Real devices you already have

The cheapest real device lab is the phones around you: your own phone, a colleague's iPhone, an old Android in a drawer. For a business website, five minutes on two or three real phones before launch catches most of what matters.

Chrome and Safari both support remote debugging, so you can inspect the page on a connected phone from your desktop. Chrome does it with an Android phone over USB, and Safari does it with an iPhone connected to a Mac.

If you test often, a small shelf of second-hand phones is worth considering: one recent iPhone, one older iPhone and one mid-range Android cover a surprising share of real visitors. Keep them on the operating system versions your analytics show, rather than updating them all to the newest.
Which free option should you use?

v: Business owner checking a site before a campaign: a real phone, plus Safari or Chrome device mode. My guide to [[testing on an iPhone without an iPhone|/how-to-use-browserstack]] covers the rest.
Developer on a Mac: Xcode Simulator for iPhone, the Android Studio emulator for Android, and Playwright for regression tests.
Developer on Windows or Linux: the Android Studio emulator, Playwright including WebKit, and a free cloud tier or trial for real iPhone checks.
Open source maintainer: BrowserStack's open source programme.
QA team with a growing suite: start with Playwright or Selenium in CI, and pay for a cloud only for the real-device coverage you cannot get any other way.

blocks.v: When free tools stop being enough, the question becomes whether a paid plan earns its cost, which I cover in [[BrowserStack pros and cons|/browserstack-pros-and-cons]]. For more everyday tooling, see my list of [[must-have developer tools|/must-have-developer-tools-for-2025]].
Frequently asked questions
Is there a completely free alternative to BrowserStack?

Not one that gives unlimited real devices. Browser device modes, Xcode Simulator, Android Studio's emulator and Playwright cover most layout and automated testing for free, and free cloud tiers give limited real-device time.
Can I test Safari on Windows for free?

Not real Safari, which only runs on Apple devices. Playwright's WebKit build runs on Windows and Linux and catches many WebKit problems, but its own documentation says it is not the same as branded Safari.
Is LambdaTest free?

LambdaTest, now called TestMu AI, has a free-forever plan as of November 2026, with short live sessions renewed monthly and a one-time allowance of 100 automation minutes. Regular testing needs a paid plan.
Are emulators good enough for testing?

For layout and most functionality, yes. For the final check before launch, test on at least one real iPhone and one real Android phone, because emulators can miss hardware and manufacturer-specific behaviour.
Is Playwright a BrowserStack alternative?
Partly. Playwright replaces the test framework and runs tests on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit for free. It does not give you real phones, which is what a cloud like BrowserStack adds.
